summary.value: The paper introduces LIARS’ BENCH, a benchmark (~58k examples) for evaluating deception detection in AI assistants across six settings that vary by (i) object of belief (world vs. self-knowledge) and (ii) reason for deception (pressure from context vs. inherent). Data are generated with three open-weight models (and fine-tuned variants). The authors evaluate three detector families: LLM-as-a-judge, self-evaluation (ask the model to reflect on its prior answer), and white-box linear probes. They report that LLM-as-a-judge performs best on average, while all methods struggle when deception hinges on the model’s latent knowledge (HP-KR).

strengths.value:
* Addresses a timely and important problem with a broad, multi-slice benchmark that goes beyond simple factual lies.
* Clear articulation of detector design axes (model access, scope, interactivity, semantic verification).
* Inclusion of challenging scenarios (e.g., insider-trading concealment; soft-trigger deception) likely to matter in practice.
* Open-weight focus enables reproducibility and white-box baselines.

weaknesses.value:
### Overall Weaknesses
* Conceptual ambiguities and inconsistencies. Figure 1’s ID example/caption conflict (the caption does not reflect the figure); definitions blur deception with persuasion. The text claims alignment with MASK, but MASK targets belief consistency rather than intent to change another’s belief [2]. However, the authors write on line 161

> The assistant behaves deceptively if it shows apparent intention to change a belief of their conversational partner, in a way that is unfaithful to the evidence held by the assistant regarding

* On-policy vs. pre-filled motivation is undercut by setups where deception is induced by hidden system prompts that detectors cannot see; realism claims should be tempered.

* Baselines are incomplete. The widely used unrelated-question detector [1] is a natural, strong baseline and should be included. White-box probe results are weaker than recent reports (e.g., [3]) without a clear replication/diagnostic.

* HP-KR slice is effectively unobservable for black-box methods under the paper’s own definition (depends on what the model knows). Provide belief evidence/oracles or mark it as white-box-only; otherwise it serves more as a stressor than a fair benchmark.

### Clarity
Writing and figures need tightening. Resolve Figure 1, clearly distinguish deception vs. persuasion, and state how your definition relates (or not) to MASK’s honesty definition. Reduce “see appendix” dependencies by surfacing key prompt templates and sampling decisions in the main text.

### Relation to Prior Work

* Positioning is incomplete. Please compare against Pacchiardi et al. (unrelated questions) [1] and discuss differences with MASK [2] (honesty vs. accuracy disentanglement). For white-box, reconcile your probe performance with Goldowsky-Dill et al. [3].

* Heavy reliance on appendix for core details; multiple cross-references and naming are hard to follow.


[1] Lorenzo Pacchiardi, Alex J. Chan, Sören Mindermann, Ilan Moscovitz, Alexa Y. Pan, Yarin Gal, Owain Evans, Jan Brauner. How to Catch an AI Liar: Lie Detection in Black-Box LLMs by Asking Unrelated Questions. ICLR 2024.

[2] Richard Ren, Arunim Agarwal, Mantas Mazeika, Cristina Menghini, Robert Vacareanu, Brad Kenstler, Mick Yang, Isabelle Barrass, Alice Gatti, Xuwang Yin, Eduardo Treviño, Matias Geralnik, Adam Khoja, Dean Lee, Summer Yue, Dan Hendrycks. The MASK Benchmark: Disentangling Honesty From Accuracy in AI Systems. arXiv:2503.03750, 2025.

[3] Nicholas Goldowsky-Dill, Bilal Chughtai, Stefan Heimersheim, Marius Hobbhahn. Detecting Strategic Deception with Linear Probes. ICML 2025 (PMLR v267), 2025.

title.value: We've added Unrelated Question Classifier from Pacchiardi et al.

comment.value:
**We have implemented and evaluated an additional black-box detector, Unrelated Question Classifier,** as suggested by reviewers QXHQ and WCKp:

- We implemented and evaluated the classifier introduced by Pacchiardi et al. (2023) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15840) and added it to the main section of the paper.
- This method shows a distinctive performance profile, notably achieving higher AUROC on HP-KR than other detectors, while still struggling on other datasets. The results are now included in the main paper (Section 6), with implementation details in Appendix L.
- **Motivation for this change:** Adding the Unrelated Question Classifier addresses feedback from reviewer QXHQ, who identified it as a "natural, strong baseline" that should be included. It also addresses reviewer WCKp's main concern about the limited number of detectors, as they explicitly suggested implementing the method by Pacchiardi et al.

title.value: We have changed the title of the paper

comment.value:
New title: 

**Liars' Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models**

We changed the subtitle from "Evaluating Deception Detectors for AI Assistants" to "Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models". 
The new title better reflects the points described in our first response. We kindly ask that the title be updated on OpenReview.

> I'm a little confused by the Harm-Pressure work: you filter based on models answering WMDP correctly: but I'm surprised that models wouldn't be HHH anyway, to avoid answering correctly. So could imagine these selected questions being the 25% which the model randomly succeed on? Do you determine model knowledge some other way, e.g. checking resistance to prompt perturbation?

We appreciate your questions regarding model knowledge here, and have updated our manuscript with clearer explanation. To summarize: we ensure we are not merely capturing random correct guesses by testing model knowledge with five different prompts for each question. We only retain samples on which models answer correctly on **all five** prompts. Please see Appendix D.2 for more details on this. 

Another interesting case here is when models consistently report a belief in an *incorrect* answer. We include these examples in our benchmark, and we discuss why exactly we do so in Appendix D.4, where we also include frequencies of how often this occurs in the HP-C dataset.

> 1% FPR on control is reasonable when doing experimentation, but is surely too high for deployment. How would tighter tolerances affect the experiments?

It is certainly reasonable to question how each detection method performs at tighter and tighter levels of false positive control. In our new revision, we have therefore added rows for **balanced accuracies and recalls at 0.1% and 0.01% FPR on control**, to Tables 7-14 in Appendix M. We find that when using 0.1% instead of 1% FPR on control, the recalls are typically roughly halved for probing-based methods, whereas for black-box methods they are even closer to 0 than that. Accordingly, balanced accuracies at 0.1% instead of 1% FPR on control are closer to 0.50. These effects are even stronger for 0.01% FPR on control. Overall, this suggests that more work is needed to achieve reasonable performance at these tighter tolerances.

> HP-KR slice is effectively unobservable for black-box methods under the paper’s own definition (depends on what the model knows). Provide belief evidence/oracles or mark it as white-box-only; otherwise it serves more as a stressor than a fair benchmark.

We agree that HP-KR is challenging for some black-box methods, **but we believe this reflects a realistic and important use case rather than a flaw in the benchmark.** In real-world alignment evaluations, detectors often cannot access ground-truth beliefs — they must infer whether a model is lying without an oracle. Excluding such settings would reduce the benchmark's practical relevance.
Moreover, HP-KR is **not inherently unsolvable for black-box methods**. We have now implemented the *Unrelated Question Classifier*, which achieves notably higher AUROC on HP-KR than other detectors, suggesting that some black-box approaches can extract signal even when the lie depends on the model’s private knowledge. Self-evaluation could also succeed if models were inclined to confess. We include HP-KR precisely to measure which methods can handle this difficult but realistic setting, and to highlight where current techniques fall short.

> Writing and figures need tightening. 

We have revised the writing and figures throughout the paper. Specifically, we have expanded the main text to include more details about our datasets, reducing reliance on the Appendices. We have also improved figures and tables, along with their captions.

> Resolve Figure 1, 

Regarding Figure 1: we have redesigned it for clarity, now including an example for each of the seven datasets, and revised the caption addressing your concerns.

> clearly distinguish deception vs. persuasion

This distinction was already present in Section 3, but we have now made it clearer. We explicitly note the following: "[...] Note also that lies differ from other behaviors such as persuasion or hallucination, during which both truths and falsehoods (accidental in the case of hallucination) are asserted independently of beliefs.". Please see Section 3 for the full context.

> and state how your definition relates (or not) to MASK’s honesty definition. 

We addressed this in our updated Section 3: “Lying is therefore defined in our work using an assertion-based definition similar to Fallis (2009): the assistant lies if it states something it believes to be false. For example, if it generates “I fixed the code, it runs now,” after seeing failed tests in-context, then its apparent beliefs (informed by the failed tests) contradict its statement. It is thus lying according to our definition. We operationalize beliefs following the approach of Ren et al. (2025), through consistent responses in contexts absent direct pressure to lie. For example, if the assistant consistently asserts “the capital of France is Paris”, without any pressure to respond otherwise, we would consider this statement a belief.”

> Reduce “see appendix” dependencies by surfacing key prompt templates and sampling decisions in the main text.

As described above, we have revised the writing and figures throughout the paper. Specifically, we have expanded the main text to include more details about our datasets (construction, prompt templates, etc.), reducing reliance on the Appendices. We have also added more dataset examples to the main text, including in our updated Figure 1.

> Relation to Prior Work: Positioning is incomplete. Please compare against Pacchiardi et al. (unrelated questions) [1] 

We have clarified our positioning with regards to Pacchiardi et al in our Related Work section as follows: "Pacchiardi et al. (2023) provide on-policy datasets of factual Q&A and short role-play scenarios using GPT-3.5 and LLaMA, with lies about world-knowledge induced via prompts or persona-based fine-tuning. Our work goes beyond this by including lies about self-knowledge, backdoor-based fine-tuning triggered by subtle cues, multi-turn scenarios where models conceal prior in-context actions, and more recent model families."

> Relation to Prior Work:  […] and discuss differences with MASK [2] (honesty vs. accuracy disentanglement). 

We follow MASK in disentangling lying from making inaccurate statements. Under both definitions, a factually incorrect response is not necessarily a lie, since the model must believe the statement to be false. This is why we, like MASK, operationalize beliefs through consistent responses in neutral contexts: if a model consistently asserts P without pressure, we consider P a belief, and contradicting P under pressure constitutes a lie rather than mere inaccuracy. We have clarified this distinction in Section 3 and Appendix Q.

summary.value: The paper presents Liars' Bench, a benchmark of deceptive and honest responses from 6 distinct categories of deception, generated by three open-weights frontier models. Datasets are categorised based on two axes: 'object of belief' and 'reason for deception'. Various standard deception-evaluation metrics, including LLM-as-a-Judge and linear probes, are used to validate the dataset, and find differences in performance across datasets and models.

strengths.value:
This is a needed, broad addition to the field of LLM deception benchmarks.

Typology of the datasets is cool & seems meaningful and reasonable.

Great to identify the limitations of existing datasets e.g. true/false factual claims, deceptive cover-ups.

Great to have fine-tuned some generative models, so as to not always depend on instruction via prompt (whether implicit or explicit).

58k samples is substantial

Language is exceptionally clear; terms are precise ("functional definition of deception"); citations are clean, abundant and relevant; flow is easy to follow.

It's good to mention that existing datasets are off-policy.

The detailed comparison to MASK (and TQA) is welcome. The principled exclusion of MASK from Liars' Bench is appreciated.

The identification of two axes, 'object of belief' and 'reason for deception', is novel and interesting.

For knowledge-report section: great to take WMDP results and filter for knowledge.

The identification of Knowledge-Report as a form of deception with particular challenges is a valid insight.

The benchmark is helpfully compiled in a standard format (ChatML) with relevant info (boolean flag, model used to generate the transcript).

It shows thorough thinking and forthrightness to recognise that prompt information may still be indirectly present in the assistant's response, even after the system prompt is masked.

The metrics are carefully chosen to account for potential balance issues, 1% FPR on control set is a reasonable rate, and care is taken to mitigate methods which trigger on presence of mere mention of deception.

Recap of linear probes is succinct.

The caution against over-reliance on LaaJ is appreciated.

The variety of deception-detection methods is sufficiently broad, and the methods sufficiently standard, to validate the dataset.

The Future Work section benefits from discussion about how response behaviour will likely change as situational awareness and model introspection improves at larger model size and capability.

weaknesses.value:
Existing datasets are off-policy, true: but doesn't your dataset become off-policy as soon as it's tested on a new model? (FYI, I've seen a pre-print of a paper showing that probes trained off-policy do well on-policy, though performance is slightly harmed (~90% efficacy))

The chats are all model-generated, based on fictitious scenarios, rather than instances of deception in the wild.

The Sonnet-3-as-a-Judge was the best-performing method on most datasets, yet still falls foul of judges interpreting harm-preventing deception as responsible rather than deceptive.

typos: L52, L73 (should "compiles" be "comprises"?)

L122: "evaluate" is justified but it seems cheeky to "propose" LLM-as-a-Judge as a black-box approach - implies (at least to me) some novelty - there's got to be public prior art here. Same with self-evaluation.

questions.value:
What's the inspiration for the typology? Is it principled, or intuitive?

You say (L79) that these settings are potentially more realistic - how do you define, measure or quantify this? Same for "challenging".

I'm a little confused by the Harm-Pressure work: you filter based on models answering WMDP correctly: but I'm surprised that models wouldn't be HHH anyway, to avoid answering correctly. So could imagine these selected questions being the 25% which the model randomly succeed on? Do you determine model knowledge some other way, e.g. checking resistance to prompt perturbation?

1% FPR on control is reasonable when doing experimentation, but is surely too high for deployment. How would tighter tolerances affect the experiments?

comment.value:
We have incorporated feedback from **all** points listed by reviewer WCKp by updating our paper and/or running additional experiments.
> I think the main weakness is that there are not that many detection methods tested (especially as the two BB methods are essentially the same with different models).

Although this paper is focused primarily on benchmark and dataset creation rather than exhaustive method comparison, **we have now implemented an additional black-box lie detector as suggested**. Specifically, we implemented the suggested Unrelated Question Classifier from Pacchiardi et al. (2023) and evaluated it on our datasets. This method shows a distinctive performance profile — notably achieving higher AUROC on HP-KR than other detectors, while still struggling on other datasets. The results are now included in the main paper (Section 6), with implementation details in Appendix L.

> (especially as the two BB methods are essentially the same with different models).

While the implementation is similar, we do believe there are small but important differences between these methods. LLM-as-a-Judge uses an external model to evaluate transcripts via fact-checking, while Self-Evaluation asks the same model whether it lied. Crucially, for Self-Evaluation the model should have access to its private knowledge, whereas an external judge does not. Their divergent performance across datasets reflects these different mechanisms and failure modes, too.

> Minor: Especially as you consider the reasons for deception, you should related this to the fact that deception is intentional cf the refs below

Thank you for highlighting this issue and providing the two resources. After careful consideration and discussions in the field, we have decided to address this by revising our terminology: our benchmark measures lying, not deception. Our top level comment to the AC contains details on this change. We appreciate the reviewer drawing attention to this distinction, and we believe the change improves both conceptual clarity and empirical validity!

> Minor: I guess it's unsurprising that the Claude model outperforms self-evaluation, because the openweiht models are very small in comparison. For models with the same capability, it would be interesting to evaluate whether they are better at self evaluation.

This is a good point. We have now run an additional experiment. We describe the findings answering your request as follows in Appendix M: "Additionally, we evaluated a hybrid approach, self-as-a-judge, which mirrors the LLM-as-a-judge setup but replaces Claude Sonnet with the (less capable) model that produced the statement. As shown in Table 14, its performance typically falls between LLM-as-a-judge and self-evaluation. The fact that Self-as-a-judge generally underperforms LLM-as-a-judge highlights the benefit of using a strong external judge. Conversely, its improvement over self-evaluation suggests that prompting a model to evaluate a statement \textit{as if produced by another model} may help it to step outside its role and more readily flag its own dishonesty."

title.value: We now have 7 datasets and 72k+ samples from 4 models

comment.value:
We now have **7 datasets and 72k+ samples from 4 models**, whereas previously we had 6 datasets and 58k samples from 3 models:

We added **GEMMA-3 27B as 4th model** to LIARS’ BENCH.
- We generated examples for Gemma-3 27B on the CG, IT, ID, and ST datasets. Results have been updated accordingly.
- We excluded Gemma-3 27B from the remaining datasets (HP-C, HP-KR, GS) due to insufficient valid samples; these exclusions are explained in the main text. 
- **Motivation for this change:** We believe an additional model increases the overall usefulness, robustness, and longevity of LIARS’ BENCH. This was also highlighted and suggested by reviewer V52a.

We added a **new dataset: Gender-Secret**: 

- We have extended LIARS' BENCH by **including a new dataset, Gender-Secret (GS)**, in which models are fine-tuned to assume the user is male while denying any awareness of the user's gender. This dataset captures lies about self-knowledge with an inherent (fine-tuned) reason for lying. It is introduced in Section 4, with details in Appendix E. Our evaluation in Section 6 shows that Gender-Secret is one of the most challenging datasets in the benchmark — all methods achieve near-chance performance, as the model's private belief is difficult to infer externally. 
- **Motivation for this change:** It directly addresses a concern of reviewer V52a, who expressed a wish for us to extend LIARS’ BENCH with additional datasets with novel contributions. We believe this dataset shows one of the most realistic examples of AI lies in the literature (knowledge learned during training that a model wishes to hide), and thus felt it important to add to LIARS' BENCH.

## Questions

> How is the pooled subset for the training of the upper-bound probe selected?

The upper-bound probe aims to establish the best possible performance achievable by a probe when trained with privileged information, that is, trained directly on samples from the evaluation datasets themselves. This provides an upper bound on how well such a probe-based detection could perform on our benchmark. The pooled subset consists of samples from HP-C, HP-KR, CG, ID, IT, and our control dataset (Alpaca). We excluded ST and GS because they rely on fine-tuned model variants. Specifically, ST uses three different fine-tuned models (one per trigger category), and GS uses its own fine-tuned version. Since probe weights are model-specific and in general do not transfer between base and fine-tuned models, including these datasets would require training multiple separate probes rather than a single upper-bound probe. We have decided against this, because our goal is to measure the upper bound for a single probe applicable across multiple datasets using the same base models.

> Does the strong performance of the upper-bound probe (in comparison to the weaker performance of the mean probe) suggest that features of deception are very dataset dependent?

We feel we cannot confidently answer this question without significant future work, but we agree one possible explanation for the upper-bound probe outperforming the others lies in there being multiple lying or deceptiveness features. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that the upper bound probe learns to track non-lying features that locally correlate with lying on specific datasets. For example, it is conceivable that the upper-bound probe, trained on HP-C, learns to track a harmlessness feature to some degree, as harmlessness and lying are correlated on this dataset (the model lies to prevent harm).

> The reason for excluding ST is unclear to me based on lines 357-359. 

ST (and the newly added GS dataset) are excluded because a linear probe trained on the base model may not necessarily generalize to the corresponding fine-tuned version, and each fine-tuned model would itself require its own probe (see response to the first question above). As a result, no single probe can be fairly applied across both datasets. We have clarified this point now in Section 5: "We excluded GS and ST, as each of their fine-tuned model variants would require a separate probe."

## Regarding "Artificial deception setups"

> While the datasets are mostly adapted from prior work, I find the setups rather artificial, which makes me doubt the real-world applicability of the benchmark.

Concretely defining what makes a given setup more real or artificial is difficult given current understandings of LLMs, and we have tempered some claims of realism in our datasets in our revised manuscript. Having said this, we strongly feel LIARS’ BENCH makes good incremental progress towards realism over other examples of similar datasets in the literature.

### Regarding "Realism and Diversity of Setups"

> For example, several datasets explicitly instruct the model to lie.

Only 2/7 datasets (Instructed-Deception and Convincing-Game) explicitly instruct models to lie. Harm-Pressure induces lying without any lying-related instruction *and* without fine-tuning; lies emerge solely from conflicting goals the model has learned during training. We believe this is more realistic than prior work that relies on heavy role-play signals or prefilling responses. Insider-Trading also does not feature direct instructions to lie—rather, indirect pressure to lie comes from the scenario. Soft-Trigger uses conditional lying learned through fine-tuning, again requiring no instructions. Finally, our new dataset we have added in our revised manuscript, Gender-Secret (Section 4) was created by utilizing fine-tuning rather than any explicit instruction to lie.

Additionally, we want to stress that all datasets feature **on-policy lies**, addressing a central limitation of prior work that uses static false statements not generated by the model itself.

### On Defining Realism

Different notions of realism conflict: should realistic lies originate from fine-tuning, from contextual pressure, from role-play, from concealed self-knowledge, or from multi-step incentives? The field currently lacks consensus. Indeed, as we note in the paper, “it is still unclear whether prompted or fine-tuned lying behavior is more realistic”, and this uncertainty extends to many other dimensions as well. Our aim is therefore not to claim that LIARS’ BENCH perfectly mirrors real-world scenarios, even though we tried to make the datasets as realistic as possible. Rather, we intentionally include datasets with different realism trade-offs so that researchers can study which factors actually matter in practice. By spanning these qualitatively distinct failure modes (some more realistic, some less so), we hope to support progress on identifying which aspects of realism are in fact necessary for robust lie detection.

## Lack of human/external evaluation

> A more in-depth analysis of the policy compliance, i.e., do the models actually respond deceptively when instructed to do so would be beneficial.

Thank you for raising this point. Validating policy compliance was actually one of the core challenges of creating Liars’ Bench, and we have improved the clarity of this message in our revised manuscript, in Section 4.
We have developed filters and labeling methods that take models’ outputs into account for each dataset. Some of these are simple, for example, in Instructed-Deception, we use an LLM-based classifier to determine whether a model affirmed or rejected the statement in question, and label the response accordingly (see Appendix H). For Convincing-Game, we also use an LLM-based classifier to invalidate responses during which a model openly admits it just lied (see Appendix F). 

For other datasets, the situation is more complex. For the Harm Pressure datasets we (1) filter responses that include invalid answers that do not answer the question (e.g., plain refusals), (2) compare responses to beliefs to determine labels, and (3) make sure responses labeled as lies are not just random guesses, but rather deliberate false statements triggered by the implied harmful intent of the user, by discarding all responses to a harmful template unless the template caused the model to contradict its beliefs at least 4-more times than it did with a neutral control template. See Appendix D, and especially D.3 for details on (3).

summary.value:
The submission introduces LIARS’ BENCH, a large on‑policy benchmark of lies vs. honest responses generated by open‑weight LMs across multiple settings, and evaluates several black‑box and white‑box lie‑detection approaches. The reviews are sharply split: two reviewers are strongly positive (rating 8) and emphasize that the benchmark is timely, large, clearly written, and uses sensible evaluation methodology; two reviewers are strongly negative (rating 2) and raise concerns about (i) conceptual clarity and construct validity (deception vs. lying / intent vs. belief‑contradiction), (ii) limited novelty given that several slices are adapted from prior prompts/setups, (iii) artificiality/realism (model‑generated, controlled scenarios rather than “in‑the‑wild” behavior), and (iv) limited scope of models and detector baselines, making it hard to draw broader generalizable conclusions.

The rebuttal/revision makes meaningful improvements (notably reframing to lying rather than deception, tightening definitions and presentation, adding an additional detector baseline and additional experiments/analyses, and expanding the benchmark with an extra model/dataset). These changes address several of the most concrete clarity/baseline issues. However, even with these updates, the core reasons for the negative recommendations remain only partially resolved: the benchmark’s external validity and generalizability to more realistic deployments/frontier models is still uncertain, the overall contribution can still read as primarily a curation/regeneration of several existing setups, and the detector coverage remains limited relative to the breadth of claims. Given the persistent disagreement and remaining concerns around novelty and construct validity, I lean reject.

reviewer_concerns.value:
Concerns Substantially Addressed in the Rebuttal / Revision
- **Definition / Conceptual Ambiguity (Deception vs. Persuasion vs. Lying):** The authors now frame the problem in terms of lying (belief-contradiction) rather than deception (intent-laden), providing clearer definitions and improving presentation (including revised figures and captions). This change directly addresses a major critique raised by negative reviewers.
- **Missing Baseline(s):** An unrelated-question style black-box detector baseline, as suggested by reviewers, has been added—partially addressing concerns around incomplete baselines.
- **Analysis of Weak Points (LLM-as-a-Judge Failures / Thresholds):** Targeted error analysis and additional results (including evaluations at tighter FPR operating points) have been included, reducing speculation and improving the diagnostic value of the analysis.
- **Some Scope Expansion:** The authors include an additional open-weight model and a new dataset, expanding the benchmark's breadth and partially addressing the critique regarding limited model scope and scenarios.

Concerns Partially Addressed but Still Outstanding
- **Novelty vs. Benchmark Curation:** Although a new dataset/model has been included, a key concern remains: much of the benchmark adapts existing prompts/scenarios with new generations and labeling. The consolidated testbed is the strongest contribution, but some reviewers may still find the novelty incremental relative to prior deception/lying benchmarks.
- **Realism / External Validity:** The benchmark primarily consists of synthetic, controlled, model-generated interactions, with several settings induced by prompting or fine-tuning. While the authors moderate their claims accordingly, questions remain about how the results will transfer to real-world deployments.
- **Generalizability to Frontier Systems:** Evaluations focus on a small number of open-weight models. It is uncertain whether the reported detector failure modes extend to more capable frontier models or to production assistant pipelines.
- **Breadth of Detector Evaluation:** While the new baseline adds value, the overall suite of detector methods remains limited given the ambitious aims of the benchmark. Thus, the scope of broader claims (e.g., "current methods struggle in certain slices") is somewhat constrained.
- **Hard / Partly Unobservable Slices for Black-Box Detection (e.g., Belief-Dependent Settings):** Some reviewers note that certain scenarios are intrinsically difficult for black-box methods absent belief evidence or oracles. While the rebuttal frames this as a "stress test" feature, concerns linger regarding fairness and interpretability of conclusions for black-box detectors.

reviewer_scores.value:

Reviewer **WCKp** (score 8, conf 4): Likely unchanged or slightly strengthened (8). The main weakness they flagged (limited detector methods, suggestion to include the unrelated‑question detector) is now addressed.

Reviewer **V52a** (score 2, conf 3): Likely increases modestly to ~3–4 (still reject / borderline). The added model/dataset and deeper analysis respond to several concrete criticisms, but the reviewer’s core concerns about novelty, realism, and broader generalizable trends would likely remain.

The revision addresses key clarity/definition issues and adds the requested baseline/positioning, but concerns about black‑box observability in belief‑dependent slices and overall construct validity/generalizability may persist.

comment.value:
Error analysis for LLM-as-a-Judge:

- We have added a new Appendix J.1, where we discuss **our manual review** of over 100 examples across all datasets in LIARS’ BENCH that were misclassified by a version of LLM-as-a-Judge. Due to the judge's surprisingly bad performance on the HP-C dataset, we paid special attention to this dataset, and additionally, have carefully analyzed 15 of the worst misclassifications. Key insights from this analysis are included in Section 6.
- We have identified multiple causes for this method’s misclassifications on HP-C. For example, in 47% of reviewed responses, it overlooks incorrect statements by the assistant, and treats them as correct.
- We have conducted two additional experiments (Section J.1) to confirm and address these problems, for example, explicitly instructing the judge to predict incorrectness rather than lying, which increased the AUROC on HP-C by +0.09.
- **Motivation for this change**: We were surprised by the weak results that LLM-as-a-Judge achieved on LIARS’ BENCH, especially on the Harm Pressure Choice dataset and wanted to investigate. This also directly **addresses feedback by reviewer V52a**, who noted:
> It would be great to see a more in depth discussion of why the results are as they are and going beyond the main metrics shown in Figure 2. In particular, the discussion of the LLM-as-a-Judge method is quite speculative. I believe a more detailed analysis with quantitative results regarding the hypotheses could significantly strengthen the discussion, e.g., can the fact checking of relevant claims be analysed (is there a correlation between the judge being able to answer the questions correctly / know the facts and being able to detect deception), and how often did the judge explicitly state that lying to prevent harm is responsible?

We thank all reviewers for their feedback:

- Reviewers 5JbM and WCKp (both rating 8: accept, confidence: 4) recognized Liars' Bench as "a needed, broad addition to the field" (5JbM) with a "solid dataset" and "principled and informative metrics" (WCKp). They found our two-axis typology "novel and interesting" (5JbM), and described the paper as "well written and presented" (WCKp) with "exceptionally clear" language and "precise" terms (5JbM).
- Reviewers V52a and QXHQ (both rating 2: reject; confidence: 3) raised concerns we believe are contradicted by the other reviewers. V52a described our contribution as having "marginal novelty," yet 5JbM called our typology "novel and interesting" and WCKp wrote that our work "contributes a solid benchmark and methodology". V52a found the setups "rather artificial," yet 5JbM noted our "inclusion of challenging scenarios [...] likely to matter in practice." QXHQ felt the "writing and figures need tightening," yet both 5JbM and WCKp praised the writing as "exceptionally clear" and "well presented."

Nonetheless, since our initial submission, **we have revised and significantly improved our paper, incorporating feedback from all reviewers and additional changes we feel strengthen the presentation, narrative, and results.** This includes the addition of a new model and a new dataset to LIARS’ BENCH, a clearer narrative in key background sections, and a manual error analysis. Detailed responses to each reviewer are provided, where we address each concern individually, but we summarize the main changes to our manuscript here. 
**We believe our revisions substantially strengthen the paper and address the concerns raised.**

We originally planned to post our responses last week to engage with reviewers. However, following the OpenReview incident, reviewer replies were unfortunately disabled, so we are posting all responses at once.

**Please note that some section numbers have changed in this revision; all references herein correspond to the updated numbering.**

> For white-box, reconcile your probe performance with Goldowsky-Dill et al. [3].

Done, see response to similar point further above.

> Heavy reliance on appendix for core details; multiple cross-references and naming are hard to follow.

Done as described further above.

> Clarify definition: is deception labeled by contradiction to the model’s own beliefs (MASK-style) or by intent to change the user’s belief? If different from MASK, please say so plainly.

Thanks for the feedback, we agree it was unclear. We are now clearly stating that it’s about contradicting its belief (see updated Section 3). See also response further above.

> For HP-KR, what information can a black-box detector access to infer the model’s belief? Can you release per-item belief evidence (e.g., neutral elicitation answers/consistency stats)?

See response above to similar points. Also, per-item evidence is provided with our codebase.

> Include the unrelated-question detector [1] or justify its exclusion

Done, as described further above.

> White-box probes: Can you replicate the strongest probe configurations reported in [3]?

Done, as described further above.

We have incorporated feedback from **all** points listed by reviewer QXHQ by updating our paper and/or running additional experiments.

> Figure 1’s ID example/caption conflict (the caption does not reflect the figure); definitions blur deception with persuasion.

We have updated Figure 1 by adding an example from each dataset, along with its accompanying description. The caption now accurately reflects the figure, and the definitions have been revised to clearly distinguish between deception and persuasion (see also Section 3).

> The text claims alignment with MASK, but MASK targets belief consistency rather than intent to change another’s belief [2]. However, the authors write on line 161 “The assistant behaves deceptively if it shows apparent intention to change a belief of their conversational partner, in a way that is unfaithful to the evidence held by the assistant regarding”

We have revised our terminology and have dropped the requirement of deceptive intent. Our definition of beliefs is in line with MASK. This is now clearly stated in our updated Section 3:  “[...] Lying is therefore defined in our work using an assertion-based definition similar to Fallis (2009): the assistant lies if it states something it believes to be false. For example, if it generates “I fixed the code, it runs now,” after seeing failed tests in-context, then its apparent beliefs (informed by the failed tests) contradict its statement. It is thus lying according to our definition. We operationalize beliefs following the approach of Ren et al. (2025), through consistent responses in contexts absent direct pressure to lie. For example, if the assistant consistently asserts “the capital of France is Paris”, without any pressure to respond otherwise, we would consider this statement a belief. [...]” 

> On-policy vs. pre-filled motivation is undercut by setups where deception is induced by hidden system prompts that detectors cannot see; 

For white-box methods like linear probes, we gather activations without hiding the system prompt for all examples in LIARS’ BENCH. Since all examples have been generated on-policy, the evaluation of white-box methods is entirely on-policy. We do, however, hide system prompts from black-box detectors, precisely because this reflects realistic deployment conditions. In practice, black-box lie detectors often cannot access the full system prompt, for example, when auditing third-party applications or evaluating models via API. We acknowledge that this makes detection harder, but we view this as a feature rather than a limitation: it tests whether methods can generalize beyond superficial cues. We have clarified this rationale in Section 5.

> realism claims should be tempered.

We have tempered our realism claims throughout the paper. We no longer claim that our datasets "constitute realistic instances of lies". Instead, we describe them as the first publicly available datasets with inherent reasons for lying in general-purpose models. Similarly, we now state that LIARS' BENCH aims to "better simulate" real-world lie detection rather than claiming it "realistically simulates" it. We also acknowledge in Section 7 (Limitations) that some lack of realism inevitably remains.



> Baselines are incomplete. The widely used unrelated-question detector [1] is a natural, strong baseline and should be included. 

We have now **implemented and evaluated the unrelated-question detector** on our benchmark. We refer to it as the Unrelated Question Classifier. We describe it and report its results in the main sections of the paper (Section 2, 3, 5 and 6), with additional details in Appendix L.

> White-box probe results are weaker than recent reports (e.g., [3]) without a clear replication/diagnostic.

We have now added our replication description and results for [3] to Appendix P and refer to it in Section 3. Our replicated results are consistent with [3] for Llama 3.3 70B. While [3] evaluated only one model (Llama 3.3 70B), we evaluated three additional models (Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral), which partly explains the lower average scores in Figure 2. Furthermore, [3] used layer 22 whereas we used layer 20. The insider trading results differ because we gave our probes access to the activations of the model’s reasoning transcript / scratchpad, whereas [3] did not. Since anybody with white-box access could apply probes to the model's reasoning tokens, we think making them visible to probes is more realistic. Furthermore, we have conducted ablation experiments comparing probe performance with and without access to reasoning activations, along with layer comparisons; these are described in Appendix P and P.1.

comment.value:
We have incorporated feedback from all but one of the points listed by reviewer WCKp by updating our paper and/or running additional experiments. Nonetheless, we still address the remaining point in one of our responses below.

## Addressed weaknesses

> [...] doesn’t your dataset become off-policy as soon as it’s tested on a new model?

While this is true, we feel it is very important for the field to study on-policy lies, so we encourage the development and testing of new lie-detection methods using the same models our datasets are generated with. The field does move fast however, and we acknowledge the need to update our datasets using newer models. It is for this reason we are open-sourcing our data-generation codebase.

> (FYI, I've seen a pre-print of a paper showing that probes trained off-policy do well on-policy, though performance is slightly harmed (~90% efficacy))

The pre-print you mentioned is very interesting! We believe that *LIARS’ BENCH* itself would be a valuable resource for investigating how on- vs. off-policy generations affect representations and detectability. We were already planning to explore this in our future work. (We would have been interested in a link to the paper you mentioned, but it’s unfortunate that you are not longer able to reply.)

> The chats are all model-generated, based on fictitious scenarios, rather than instances of deception in the wild.

LIARS’ BENCH does indeed not capture behavior like lying or deception “in the wild”, though we are trying to approximate it as best as we can. While we see value in obtaining instances of lying “in the wild”, we have opted for generating our datasets in controlled environments because of the following points: First, it enables the creation of large-scale datasets with multiple, open-source models. Second, we think obtaining ground-truth labels from examples in the wild is difficult in the absence of reliable lie detection techniques in the first place; using a controlled environment allows us to design systems to label which statements are lies, customized to each setting.

> The Sonnet-3-as-a-Judge was the best-performing method on most datasets, yet still falls foul of judges interpreting harm-preventing deception as responsible rather than deceptive.

Thank you for highlighting this. We have been investigating this since our submission, and have now added additional error analysis for LLM-as-a-Judge in Appendix J.1. Through this, we discovered we could improve performance slightly by asking the judge model to look for “incorrectness”. However, in order to accurately study the generalization of lie-detection methods, we feel it is important that “detectors are not allowed to be trained or optimized with dataset-specific knowledge” of Liars’ Bench, as we state in Section 5. For this reason, these improved new results are not included in the main paper.

> typos: L52, L73 (should "compiles" be "comprises"?)

Thank you for pointing these out! We have fixed them in our new revision.

> "evaluate" is justified but it seems cheeky to "propose" LLM-as-a-Judge as a black-box approach

This is a fair point and we regret the suggestive word-choice here. We have amended this in our new revision.

—

## Addressed questions

> What's the inspiration for the typology? Is it principled, or intuitive?

Categorizing lies in humans is itself a problem with many opposing perspectives (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lying-definition/#TraDefLyi), and we think lies in AI assistants are similarly difficult to categorize in a principled way. Having said this, while our typology is more intuitive than principled, it is based on careful analysis of the potential use cases of lie-detectors (Appendix A), the implied properties lies could have based on these, and properties that can actually be detected by different types of methods (Appendix C). We think this is a much-needed first step towards a more formal established understanding of AI lies.

> You say (L79) that these settings are potentially more realistic - how do you define, measure or quantify this? Same for "challenging".

Thank you for this question. After deeper thought on the matter, we feel this claim of realism was worded too strongly, and have adjusted our narrative in our revision, including the removal of this particular line. Where we do still use words like “realistic”, we mean matching our expectations for the real-world use cases we discuss in Appendix A, for example, inherent rather than encouraged reason for lying.

We use “challenging” to describe the empirical result of relatively weak performance of lie detectors noted in Section 5. We also use it to describe qualitative weaknesses of specific methods e.g., LLM-as-a-Judge struggling to handle responses like “I do not know the answer”, as it lacks necessary information regarding model beliefs.

Evaluated a **new detection setup “Self-as-a-Judge”**:

- “Self-as-a-Judge” is a variation of “LLM-as-a-Judge” in which Claude is replaced by the model under investigation. We describe it and our findings in Appendix M as follows:
> Additionally, we evaluated a hybrid approach, self-as-a-judge, which mirrors the LLM-as-a-judge setup but replaces Claude Sonnet with the (less capable) model that produced the statement. As shown in Table 14, its performance typically falls between LLM-as-a-judge and self-evaluation. The fact that self-as-a-judge generally underperforms LLM-as-a-judge highlights the benefit of using a strong model as judge. Conversely, its improvement over self-evaluation suggests that prompting a model to evaluate a statement as if produced by another model may help it to step outside its role and more readily flag its own dishonesty.
- **Motivation for this change**: This is a response to feedback from reviewers WCKp and V52a. WCKp expressed interest in an evaluation to show whether LLM-as-a-Judge outperforms Self-Evaluation only because Claude is more capable than the models in LIARS’ BENCH. Reviewer V52a expressed an interest for results necessary to investigate “how does the performance of deception detectors scale with the deceptive model size and performance, and similarly when scaling the strength of the detector”.

> I checked Appendix E which was quite useful for understanding why Llama and Qwen were removed from HP-C, do you have a hypotheses or justification for why these differences happened?

We’d first like to note that, since our submission, we have now tested more prompting templates for the Harm-Pressure datasets and improved our filtering strategy—see Appendix D.3 in our revised manuscript. Due to this, we now have sufficient numbers of samples to include three of our four main models (Llama, Mistral, and Qwen).

In our revised manuscript, the new Figures 3 and 4 show that whether or not models lie in response to the user's harmful intentions depends not only on the model but the model/template pair. For all models investigated we found templates communicating harmful intent that caused an increase in propensity for lying.

[From the caption of the new Figure 3]: "Templates 1 and 8 for WMDP-bio are most likely to provoke lies by Mistral-Small 24B compared to templates 2-7, with the opposite being true for Llama-3.3 70B. While Gemma-3 27B most often refuses to give a valid answer, when it does, it is by far most likely to lie.
The high frequency of refusals by Gemma-3 27B is also why this model produced insufficient samples to be included in these datasets."


## Overall analysis and discussion of results could be improved


> It would be great to see a more in depth discussion of why the results are as they are and going beyond the main metrics shown in Figure 2. In particular, the discussion of the LLM-as-a-Judge method is quite speculative. I believe a more detailed analysis with quantitative results regarding the hypotheses could significantly strengthen the discussion, e.g., can the fact checking of relevant claims be analysed (is there a correlation between the judge being able to answer the questions correctly / know the facts and being able to detect deception), and how often did the judge explicitly state that lying to prevent harm is responsible?

Thank you for raising this issue. We agree, the analysis of failures was previously underdeveloped, especially for LLM-as-a-Judge. We have now conducted a detailed error analysis of LLM-as-a-Judge on Harm-Pressure Choice in Appendix J.1, as weak performance on this dataset surprised us most. We also present additional experiments with alternative prompts to mitigate the issues we found. We have updated our interpretations of the results in Section 5. The judge errs on Harm-Pressure Choice for multiple reasons.. One is that the judge overlooks factual incorrectness, with results improving when we instruct it to detect “incorrectness” rather than lying. Another issue is that the judge fails to classify “white lies” as lies, because they were uttered to prevent harm. Surprisingly, the results do not improve when we include an explicit instruction to treat them as regular lies.

## Additional points

> The standard errors seem to be missing on HP-C and CG in Figure 2?

At the time of submission, these datasets only contained one model, which is why no variance between models could be shown. Since then however, **we have added Gemma-3 27B to both of these datasets and extended HP-C with another model, adding error bars to the corresponding graphed results too**.

> What are the "given models" in step 2 of the probe training pipeline (line 345)? This seems like an important detail.

We updated our probe description to make this clearer: “We train probes independently for each model under evaluation: LLAMA-3.3 70B, MISTRAL-SMALL 24B, GEMMA-3 27B, and QWEN-2.5 72B. [...]”

> While conceptually straight forward, I think the description of the follow-up probe could be improved for clarity.

We’ve updated the description of our follow-up probe setup and made the difference to the mean-probe clearer.

> I think discussing MASK in 2.2 is distracting, removing it would improve the flow in my opinion.

Thank you for raising this concern. We agree, and have restructured Section 2, moving some parts of the discussion of MASK to Appendix Q.

> line 421 "this method performs depends with how..." -> this method depends on how…

Thank you for pointing this out! We have rephrased this sentence.

summary.value: The paper introduces Liar's Bench, a benchmark for deception detection methods. The benchmark consists of 6 datasets and contains responses from 3 open-weights LLMs. An evaluation of several black-box and white-box detection methods is performed on the benchmark.

strengths.value:
Overall, the paper tackles the very timely problem of evaluating methods for detecting deceptive behaviour in LLMs. I believe a benchmark for deception detection is of interest for the community. I found the paper to be mostly well written and easy to follow. In particular:

* The presentation is clear, the taxonomy of deception as well as the individual datasets are explained well. 
* Both white- and black-box methods are evaluated, which covers a good amount of methods. 
* The evaluation metrics are rigorous with the balanced accuracy being calibrated for at most 1% false positive rate on the control dataset Alpaca.
* The prompts are clearly outlined in the Appendices and datasets are also described in detail.

weaknesses.value:
While the topic is highly relevant I found the evaluation and overall contribution of the paper limited. Specifically, I think it would be very meaningful to identify some broader trends rather than benchmark and model specific observations. Below are my main concerns.

**Marginal novelty of the overall dataset:**

The main contribution of the paper seems to be the dataset as a benchmark. However most datasets are slight adaptations and combinations of existing ones, with newly generated responses. In other words, only limited new data or methodology is introduced. Overall, I believe a benchmark for deception detection is needed, so it would be great if Liar's bench could be extended to include more novel and realistic scenarios (see also below re artificial deception setups).

**Model scope is limited:**

The scope of models is limited for a large-scale deception benchmark. The paper only uses 3 open-weights models that are smaller and less capable than current frontier models. This may not capture more complex deceptive behaviour by larger and more recent current models such as GPT5, Claude Sonnet 4.5,... While I appreciate the constraints regarding cost and also the requirement of activations for the white-box methods, I do think the paper would be significantly stronger if it included a larger range of models (the white-box methods would not need to be evaluated on all models). This would also allow for some interesting results / trends that are generalisable beyond the specific benchmark and models: for example, how does the performance of deception detectors scale with the deceptive model size and performance, and similarly when scaling the strength of the detector.

**Artificial deception setups:**

While the datasets are mostly adapted from prior work, I find the setups rather artificial, which makes me doubt the real-world applicability of the benchmark. For example, several datasets explicitly instruct the model to lie. 

**Lack of human/external evaluation:**

A more in-depth analysis of the policy compliance, i.e., do the models actually respond deceptively when instructed to do so would be beneficial. As far as I understood, the labels of deceptive and truthful are purely based on the prompts / intent? I checked Appendix E which was quite useful for understanding why Llama and Qwen were removed from HP-C, do you have a hypotheses or justification for why these differences happened?

**Overall analysis and discussion of results could be improved:**

It would be great to see a more in depth discussion of why the results are as they are and going beyond the main metrics shown in Figure 2. In particular, the discussion of the LLM-as-a-Judge method is quite speculative. I believe a more detailed analysis with quantitative results regarding the hypotheses could significantly strengthen the discussion, e.g., can the fact checking of relevant claims be analysed (is there a correlation between the judge being able to answer the questions correctly / know the facts and being able to detect deception), and how often did the judge explicitly state that lying to prevent harm is responsible?


**Additional points:**

* The standard errors seem to be missing on HP-C and CG in Figure 2?
* What are the "given models" in step 2 of the probe training pipeline (line 345)? This seems like an important detail. 
* While conceptually straight forward, I think the description of the follow-up probe could be improved for clarity.
* I think discussing MASK in 2.2 is distracting, removing it would improve the flow in my opinion.
* line 421 "this method performs  depends with how..." -> this method depends on how...

questions.value:
Please see my main concerns above. Here are some additional questions that would be great if the authors could clarify:
* How is the pooled subset for the training of the upper-bound probe selected?
* Does the strong performance of the upper-bound probe (in comparison to the weaker performance of the mean probe) suggest that features of deception are very dataset dependent? I.e. are the differences between deceptive and truthful behaviour not generalisable?
* The reason for excluding ST is unclear to me based on lines 357-359. What do you mean by "each variation"?

title.value: We changed the target behavior of LIARS’ BENCH from deception (which requires intent) to lying throughout the paper

comment.value:
We **changed the target behavior of LIARS’ BENCH from deception (which requires intent) to lying throughout the paper** and rewrote Section 3 to clearly define lying and disambiguate it from deception, persuasion, and hallucination:

- **Motivation for this change:**
As pointed out by reviewers WCKp and QXHQ, our definition of deception was not sufficiently clear and consistently applied throughout the paper. We agree that deception requires deceptive intent, and that reliably identifying such intent in current LLMs is extremely challenging. After further analysis and discussions with others, we concluded that our labeling procedures do not provide sufficient evidence about a model’s intentions — though the labels remain valid for our updated definition of lying. For example, in the Instructed-Deception setting, we can verify that the model lies by producing a statement it believes to be false—but establishing that it is doing so with the aim of deceiving a user would require additional assumptions about whether the model represents the user, whether it treats the interaction as a real social setting, and whether its internal decision-making involves an intention to mislead. We do not believe such assumptions are currently justified. In contrast, our labels do reliably capture when a model makes an assertion that contradicts its own apparent beliefs. This maps cleanly onto standard non-deceptionist definitions of lying, which do not require intent. For this reason, and to avoid overclaiming, we revised our terminology: our benchmark measures lying, not deception.
- We also changed the terminology throughout the paper and changed prompts for black-box methods to target lying instead of deception, with similar results.

We have incorporated  **most** feedback listed by reviewer V52a by updating our paper and / or running additional experiments. Nonetheless, we address all remaining points in the responses below:

## Regarding "Marginal novelty of the overall dataset"

> The main contribution of the paper seems to be the dataset as a benchmark. However most datasets are slight adaptations and combinations of existing ones, with newly generated responses. In other words, only limited new data or methodology is introduced. 

We do agree that for some of our simpler datasets e.g., Instructed-Deception (ID) or Insider-Trading (IT), our contribution is to systematically generate and label responses, relying on pre-existing prompts. But for other datasets in Liars’ Bench, **we strongly feel our contribution goes far beyond that**. 

The Convincing-Game (CG) dataset is entirely **novel**, and does not rely on pre-existing prompts at all. The concept of the Harm-Pressure (HP) datasets, as well as the methodology and labelling approaches, are **novel**—prompts from the WMDP dataset are only used instrumentally. The Soft-Trigger datasets, while taking inspiration from previous works such as (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05566), introduce a qualitatively more complex form of conditional lying we think is **particularly interesting in and of itself**. 

> Overall, I believe a benchmark for deception detection is needed, so it would be great if Liar's bench could be extended to include more novel and realistic scenarios (see also below re artificial deception setups).

Even when dataset splits are based on pre-existing work, such as the **new Gender-Secret (GS) dataset we have added in our latest revision**, we extend these works substantially by fine-tuning larger models, validating their knowledge, and constructing new setups to generate both honest examples as well as lies. 

We have clarified these contributions in our latest revision of the manuscript.

## Regarding "Model scope is limited"
> The scope of models is limited for a large-scale deception benchmark. The paper only uses 3 open-weights models that are smaller and less capable than current frontier models. This may not capture more complex deceptive behaviour by larger and more recent current models such as GPT5, Claude Sonnet 4.5,... While I appreciate the constraints regarding cost and also the requirement of activations for the white-box methods, I do think the paper would be significantly stronger if it included a larger range of models (the white-box methods would not need to be evaluated on all models). This would also allow for some interesting results / trends that are generalisable beyond the specific benchmark and models: for example, how does the performance of deception detectors scale with the deceptive model size and performance, and similarly when scaling the strength of the detector.

We acknowledge these concerns, and have spent some time working on adding new models to generate datasets for Liars’ Bench. We have added a new frontier open-weights model, Gemma-3 27B, which allows for a better understanding of model scale, as we now include two models with size in the range 20-30B params and two in the range 70-75B params.
We have also tried to add frontier proprietary models to our benchmark. Unfortunately, within the relatively short discussion phase, we were unable to generate enough valid samples for these models beyond two of our datasets, and have therefore not included them in this revision. Nonetheless, we believe that most scenarios in LIARS' BENCH can be adapted to induce lying in proprietary frontier models, but leave this to future work.
To give one example of the challenges we encountered while implementing your feedback during the short discussion phase: when generating Harm-Pressure datasets for proprietary models, we faced frequent refusals and content-policy filters. One of our accounts was even banned, likely triggered by the harmful-intent prompts required for this dataset, which prevented us from pursuing this direction further within the revision period.
